statement: In people who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London, frequent ketamine use compared with no ketamine use is associated with lower scores on some memory and planning tests, but not on others, when people are tested within days of their last use; in the largest study people who used ketamine less often did not score lower, but in a smaller field study a group who used it from once a month to twice a week did, three days after a night of use. Whether ketamine causes the differences is unknown. In the largest comparison (Morgan et al., 2009; five groups of 30, one session after a required 24 hours without psychotropic drugs), people who used ketamine more than four times a week (19 of 30 said daily), tested a mean of 1.6 days after last use (range 1 to 7; the follow-up paper gives a mean of 2 days, SD 2.60 rather than 1.27, for the same session), solved fewer planning problems in the fewest moves (7.66 against 8.89 to 9.53) and recognised fewer patterns (about 83% against 90% to 95%, editors' reading of a figure) than each of the other four groups, which included 30 people who used other drugs but not ketamine and 30 who used no illicit drugs, and made more errors on a spatial working-memory task (about 32 against 11 to 19, editors' reading of a figure; the paper does not say against which groups this difference was tested); their word recognition was lower too, although the editors could reproduce only one of the reported pairwise differences from the printed table. Story recall, letter and category fluency, a response-inhibition test and memory for which voice spoke a word did not differ, and people who used ketamine less often (a mean of 3.25 days a month, last use a mean of 11.3 days before) and people who had stopped did not differ from the controls on any test. The frequent group had fewer years of education (12.27 against 14.23 to 15.33), a lower vocabulary-test estimate of earlier ability (45.67 against 47.13 to 51.53) and more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 against 1 to 3), none adjusted for, and it was tested so soon after use that withdrawal or other after-effects of recent use cannot be excluded (the authors raise withdrawal). A year later (Morgan et al., 2010b; the same people, 25 of the 30 retested), averaged over both sessions the frequent group still made more spatial working-memory errors than every other group and recognised fewer patterns than the groups who used ketamine less often or had stopped, with no difference from the two control groups reported; but its mean errors fell from 29.58 to 19.92 and its pattern recognition rose from 83.68% to 89.04%, close to the controls' 88.41% and 89.58% (changes the paper did not test), and its planning score improved into the other groups' range, although 22 of the 25 were still using ketamine at least monthly. Two smaller field studies by the same team, which tested people three days after a night of use, found lower story recall and category fluency: in a group who used ketamine from once a month to twice a week, against peers with little or no ketamine use (Curran & Morgan, 2000), and in people who used it more than twice a month (a reported 13.53 days a month) against people who used it less (Curran & Monaghan, 2001), a comparison in which the more frequent group had less schooling and already had lower letter fluency on the night of use. The larger study did not find these differences. The 2000 paper itself attributes its day-3 story-recall difference to missed practice in a design that tested people while intoxicated first; its practice checks do not separate the category-naming and sentence-judging differences from missed practice either (sentence judging by the editors' recalculation); and the larger study's authors extend the explanation to the earlier story-recall differences. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In one London team's studies, people who used ketamine more than four times a week, tested a day or a few days after they last used it, did worse than people who used other drugs or none on some memory and planning tasks, such as remembering which boxes they had already searched and recognising patterns. They did as well at remembering a story and at naming words. In this study, people who used ketamine a few times a month did as well as everyone else. The frequent group also had less schooling and lower scores on a vocabulary test, and more of them had family members with mental illness, so the tests cannot show that ketamine caused the difference. A year later, the same people's scores had moved closer to the others', even though most were still using. Earlier, smaller studies that tested people three days after a night out found lower story and word scores, even in a group who used ketamine a few times a month, compared with people who hardly used it; part of this may be because they remembered little of the first test and so had less practice.
population: People who use ketamine and other drugs, studied by one research group at University College London: five groups of 30 recruited from the unit's database and by word of mouth (25 of the 30 frequent participants retested a year later), and two smaller samples recruited at parties, nightclubs and squat parties
exposure: Frequent ketamine use (more than four times a week in the main study; more than twice a month in one field study), by self-report checked with hair analysis in the main study; less frequent use (at least once a month and less than four times a week)
comparator: 30 people who used other drugs but not ketamine and 30 who used no illicit drugs, tested the same way; in the field studies, peers with little or no ketamine use, or people who used ketamine twice a month or less
outcome: Memory, planning and attention test scores in sessions without intoxication: at least 24 hours (a mean of 1.6 days, range 1 to 7, for the frequent group) after last use in the main study, 3 days after a night of use in the field studies
magnitude: Morgan et al. (2009), 30 per group, frequent group tested 1.6 days (range 1–7; 2 days, SD 2.60, by the follow-up paper) after last use: spatial working-memory errors about 32 against about 11–19 (editors' reading of Figure 1; F(4, 145) = 8.05); strategy 32.73 against 26.53–28.93; Stockings problems in minimum moves 7.66 against 8.89–9.53 (F(4, 145) = 6.58); pattern recognition about 83% against about 90–95% (editors' reading of Figure 2; F(4, 145) = 6.37); word recognition d′ 2.36 against 2.67–2.97 (F(4, 145) = 2.74; only the difference from the ex-ketamine group reproduces, editors' recalculation). No differences: story recall (immediate 8.11–8.32), letter fluency (15.14–17.53), category fluency (14.73–17.27), Hayling test. Infrequent (3.25 days a month) and ex-ketamine groups: no differences from controls. Confounders: education 12.27 against 14.23–15.33 years; spot-the-word 45.67 against 47.13–51.53; family history of mental illness 8 of 30 against 1–3. Morgan et al. (2010b), 25 of 30 frequent retested (mean interval 366.6 days for all retested participants): errors 29.58 to 19.92 (other groups 11.48–18.32, then 12.48–15.89); pattern recognition 83.68% to 89.04% (controls 88.41% and 89.58% at follow-up; averaged over both sessions lower than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups only; mean changes not tested); Stockings 7.67 to 9.50 (others 9.33–9.87 at follow-up). Field studies, 3 days after use: category fluency 14.85 against 19.68 (2000) and 14.06 against 18.95 (2001); story recall 7.75 against 10.18 (2000) and 4.56 against 9.16 (2001); sentences correctly judged 63.30 against 79.11 (2000; practice check printed p<0.009, p ≈ 0.04 on the editors' recalculation); the 2000 ketamine group used ketamine from once a month to twice a week.

evidence.locator: Method › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and Procedure, 1st paragraph (p. 78); Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph (p. 80)
evidence.extracted: 150 people in five groups of 30: frequent ketamine use (more than four times a week), infrequent use (less than four times a week but at least once a month), ex-ketamine (abstinent for at least 1 month), polydrug controls said to be matched to the current-use groups on other drugs, and controls who took no illicit drugs; recruited from the unit's own database of participants and by snowball sampling; people who used drugs had to abstain from psychotropic drugs for at least 24 hours before the single test session; urine and hair samples were collected.

evidence.locator: Results › Drug use data › Ketamine use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 80); Table 2 (p. 81)
evidence.extracted: Reported use: frequent group 20.13 (2.36) days a month, last use 1.6 (1.27) days before testing (range 1–7), 19 of the 30 reporting daily use; infrequent group 3.25 (2.55) days a month, last use 11.3 (9.36) days before (range 1–28). Hair ketamine (3 cm, about the previous 3 months): 282.14 (566.53) ng/mm in the frequent and 18.01 (41.06) in the infrequent group, none detected in either control group. Editors' note: a mean of 20.13 days with an SD of 2.36 cannot be reconciled with daily use by 19 of 30 (card sc_morgan_2009, reporting issues).

evidence.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Spatial working memory (Fig. 1) (p. 81, continuing on p. 82), Stockings of Cambridge (Table 5) and Pattern recognition memory (Fig. 2) (p. 82); Figures 1 and 2 (pp. 82–83); Table 5 (p. 83)
evidence.extracted: Groups differed in spatial working-memory errors (F(4, 145) = 8.05) and strategy (F(4, 145) = 5.00), in Stockings of Cambridge problems solved in the minimum number of moves (F(4, 145) = 6.58) and in pattern recognition (F(4, 145) = 6.37): the frequent group made more errors (P < 0.01; the text names no comparison groups for this result) and had a poorer (higher) strategy score (32.73 (5.77) against 26.53 to 28.93), solved fewer problems (7.66 (1.61) against 8.89 to 9.53) and recognised fewer patterns (P < 0.01) than each of the other groups. Editors' reading of Figures 1 and 2: about 32 errors against about 11 to 19, and about 83% against about 90% to 95% correct; editors' recalculation from Table 5 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): the Stockings differences all reproduce, the strategy difference from the polydrug controls does not (P ≈ 0.11).

evidence.locator: Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Source memory task (Table 5) (p. 82); Table 5 (p. 83)
evidence.extracted: Word recognition (d′) on the source memory task differed between groups (F(4, 145) = 2.74, P = 0.031): frequent 2.36 (0.74) against 2.67 to 2.97 in the other groups, reported as lower than all of them (P < 0.05); response bias and source errors did not differ. Editors' recalculation from Table 5 (pooled SD, Bonferroni for 10 comparisons): only the difference from the ex-ketamine group reproduces (P ≈ 0.02); against the non-drug controls P ≈ 0.11 even without correction.

evidence.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 77); Results › Neurocognitive assessments › Prose recall, Fluency and Hayling test (p. 82, continuing on p. 83); Table 5 (p. 83)
evidence.extracted: No group differences in story recall (only a main effect of delay, F(1, 145) = 34.37; immediate means 8.11 to 8.32 idea units), letter fluency (15.14 to 17.53 words) or category fluency (14.73 to 17.27; frequent group 16.84 (4.80), non-drug controls 14.73 (3.99)), and none on the Hayling test (overall 6.76 to 7.31) or on its response-inhibition part. The abstract nevertheless lists category fluency among the frequent group's impairments, which the Results and Table 5 contradict.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 84, continuing on p. 85); Discussion › Neurocognitive function, 1st paragraph (p. 85)
evidence.extracted: The authors report no differences on the neuropsychological tests between the infrequent or ex-ketamine groups and the two control groups. They state that story recall was unaffected, unlike in their earlier studies, which tested people while intoxicated and again 3 days later and whose story recall deficits may simply reflect a lack of practice effects, and that recreational use, on average 3 days a month in this study, was not associated with impaired cognitive function.

evidence.locator: Procedure (p. 78); Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph, and Table 1 (p. 80); Results › Correlations, 2nd paragraph (p. 84); Discussion › Psychological wellbeing, 1st paragraph (p. 85); Neurocognitive function, 5th paragraph, and Limitations, 1st paragraph (p. 86)
evidence.extracted: The frequent group had fewer years of education (12.27 (4.84) against 14.23 to 15.33; F(4, 145) = 4.07, P = 0.004), a lower spot-the-word estimate of premorbid ability (45.67 (6.13) against 47.13 to 51.53; F(4, 145) = 7.29) and more family history of mental illness (8 of 30 against 1 to 3; χ²(4) = 12.59, P = 0.013), none adjusted for in the group comparisons; within the frequent group word recognition correlated with spot-the-word scores (r = 0.474), while years of education correlated with none of the cognitive measures. The authors state that pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out without prospective studies, that the family history may have contributed, and that the frequent group's impairments could reflect a withdrawal state.

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Participants and design, last paragraph (p. 122); Results › Ketamine use (Table 2), 1st paragraph (p. 124); Table 2 (p. 125); Results › Cognitive assessments (Table 3) › Spatial Working Memory task, Stockings of Cambridge task, Pattern recognition memory and Prose recall (p. 126); Table 3 (p. 127)
evidence.extracted: Of the same participants, 25 of the 30 in the frequent group were retested (mean interval for all retested participants 366.6 (92.11) days); reported ketamine use changed little (no effect of time; 16.0 (10.01) days a month at follow-up, 22 of 25 still using at least monthly). Averaged over both sessions the frequent group still made more spatial working-memory errors than all other groups (group F(4,108) = 4.16, printed P = 0.04) and recognised fewer patterns than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups (printed F(1,108) = 4.429, P = 0.002), but its errors fell from 29.58 (19.93) to 19.92 (17.56), against 11.48 to 18.32 at the first session and 12.48 to 15.89 a year later in the other groups, and its pattern recognition rose from 83.68% (10.27) to 89.04% (7.24), against 88.41% (polydrug) and 89.58% (non-drug) at follow-up; its strategy score improved (31.63 to 27.33, P = 0.003) and its Stockings score rose from 7.67 to 9.50 (P = 0.003), inside the other groups' follow-up range (9.33 to 9.87); story recall showed no group effects. Editors' calculation: F(4,108) = 4.16 corresponds to P ≈ 0.004.

evidence.locator: Results › Demographics and drug use › Reported general drug use (p. 580, right column); Table 1 (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks › Category generation (p. 583, continuing on p. 584), Speed of comprehension test and Serial sevens (p. 584); Discussion › Cognitive effects, 5th paragraph (p. 586)
evidence.extracted: 3 days after a night of use, the ketamine group, which reported using ketamine from twice a week (12%) to once a month (12%), still named fewer category members (14.85 (3.08) against 19.68 (4.58)) and judged fewer sentences (63.30 (16.04) against 79.11 (19.94)) than peers with little or no ketamine use, both differences also present on the night (category fluency group F(1,37) = 21.1, no interaction); story recall was still lower (immediate 7.75 against 10.18), which the authors attribute to missed practice; serial sevens and cancellation no longer differed.

evidence.locator: Results › Demographics and reported drug use, 1st paragraph (p. 753); Table 1 and Table 2 (p. 754)
evidence.extracted: 3 days after a night of use, people using ketamine more than twice a month (a reported 13.53 days a month) recalled 4.56 (1.96) and 4.39 (1.57) story ideas immediately and after a delay and named 14.06 (3.83) category members, against 9.16 (3.86), 8.05 (4.05) and 18.95 (4.45) in people using it twice a month or less (0.45 days a month); letter fluency was lower in the more frequent group on the night as well as on day 3 (10.39 against 17.42; 14.00 against 22.10); none of the more frequent group and 4 of the less frequent group held a degree.

As summarized by the review (second-hand, by two of the same authors): infrequent or recreational use does not appear to be associated with long-term cognitive impairment; profound short- and long-term memory impairment in frequent use is called the most robust finding, citing the authors' own earlier review; many studies were cross-sectional and cannot address causation; and in a longitudinal study frequent use is said to have caused impairments of visual recognition and spatial working memory that correlated with changes in use over 12 months, a causal verb the observational design does not support, attached to the wrong reference number. Editors' note: see the review's card, sc_morgan_2012, reporting issues.

evidence.locator: Methods › Statistical analyses and rationale for comparisons (p. 579, right column); Table 1 (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks › Category generation (continued) and Speed of comprehension test (p. 584, left column)
evidence.extracted: To check for missed practice, the ketamine group's day-3 scores were compared with the comparison group's first-night scores, with significance set at p<0.01 (p. 579). For category fluency this check showed no significant difference (p. 584). For sentences correctly judged the paper prints p<0.009 for the ketamine group's day-3 score, 63.30 (16.04), against the comparison group's first-night score, 76.05 (21.45); the editors' recalculation from Table 1 (independent t-test, pooled SD, n 20 and 19) gives t(37) = 2.11, p ≈ 0.04, about the same as for category fluency, 14.85 (3.08) against 17.74 (5.39), t(37) = 2.07, p ≈ 0.046.

evidence.locator: Materials and Methods › Participants and design, 2nd paragraph (p. 122, right column); Table 2, ketamine rows, frequent group, initial session (p. 125); Discussion › Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph (p. 131, continuing on p. 132)
evidence.extracted: For the same first session that Morgan et al. (2009) report, Table 2 gives the frequent group's days since last ketamine use (n = 30) as 2 (SD 2.60); the bracketed values printed beside it, (1–14), are labelled a range, but many such values in this table cannot be ranges (card sc_morgan_2010b, reporting issues). The authors state that they could not verify the 24 hours without psychotropic drugs before testing with biological samples, because ketamine stays in urine for 1 to 2 days, and that the experimenters judged that no one appeared intoxicated. Editors' comparison: the 2009 paper gives 1.6 (SD 1.27), range 1–7, for the same session (its Table 2, p. 81).

risk_of_bias.note: Education, premorbid ability and family history of mental illness differ and are not adjusted for; testers knew the groups; recruitment partly from the unit's own database; exposure self-reported, checked by hair for ketamine only; the 24 hours without psychotropic drugs before testing could not be verified, and the frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days after use by one report of the session (a mean of 2 days with a wider spread by the other); several post hoc results in the 2009 tables cannot be reproduced; 5 of the 30 frequent participants were not retested at one year (cards sc_morgan_2009 and sc_morgan_2010b: ROBINS-E high; sc_curran_2000 and sc_curran_2001: very high).

inconsistency.note: The studies agree in direction, but not on which tests differ: story recall and category fluency were lower three days after a night of use in both field studies and did not differ in the larger study; the larger study's spatial working-memory and pattern-recognition differences narrowed over a year in people still using. The 2000 field study's ketamine group used ketamine at the frequency the larger study calls infrequent (once a month to twice a week), yet scored lower three days after a night of use, while the larger study's infrequent group did not.

indirectness.note: The comparison is the one asked about; how soon after use people were tested (1 to 7 days, 3 days) is stated for each result.

imprecision.note: 30 per group (25 retested), 18 to 20 per group in the field studies; the null results (story recall, fluency) do not exclude moderate differences, and several of the reported pairwise differences depend on the analysis.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all studies are from one group.

dose_response.note: Differences appear in the most frequent group only and not in people using a few times a month, but the groups also differ in education and family history, and the one-year correlations between change in amount and change in scores are weaker in the plotted data than in the text (card sc_morgan_2010b); no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Less education and lower premorbid estimates in the frequent group would more plausibly enlarge than hide the differences; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low. Overlapping evidence: Morgan et al. (2009) and (2010b) report the same participants and count once; the two field studies are separate samples from the same laboratory; the 2009 sample came partly from the unit's database, so overlap with the earlier samples cannot be excluded. Status mixed rather than replicated by the same team: every comparison points the same way (lower scores with frequent use on some tests), but which tests differ is inconsistent between the field studies and the larger study, and the proposed explanation (missed practice in the two-session design) fits the 2000 paper's own practice checks but cannot be separated from other explanations in these designs. Rated as worded, an association; whether it lasts or reverses after stopping is the separate, contested claim on what happens after people cut down or stop (section 9). The narrative review (Morgan & Curran, 2012) is used only to qualify, and its causal wording is not adopted.
